title: Which cutoff keeps the program?

beats.say: Follow the paper through the reader. There’s the header of our Python function. Four spaces put return inside it. We want the model to see programs like this one. The classifier scores the whole program point seven. The menu underneath scores point one.
We keep a record if its score reaches the cutoff. Which cutoff drops the menu and keeps the program, point five or point eight five?

Try point five. The menu drops out. Record C stays on the feed with all one hundred twenty of its tokens. We see just two lines of it here. Before moving the cutoff again, put your finger on the record that would disappear at point eight five.

Now slide the cutoff to point eight five. It passes the program too. That was the only code record in this little batch. If a coding score later falls, we have a lead. To test it, we'll need this record's identity, the tokens that reached training, and a fair comparison.

title: How many tokens must the corpus supply?

beats.say: Each time the model predicts a token from its prefix, the training stream has supplied another example. How many token presentations should we plan for? In this dense Chinchilla-style example, seventy billion parameters times twenty presentations per parameter gives one point four trillion. Show the same tokens again and they count again. Tokens per batch determine how many optimizer updates that volume buys.

Our article estimates dominant dense matrix arithmetic as six times parameter count times token presentations. That gives five point eight eight times ten to the twenty-three FLOPs for this plan. Keep the token count fixed and put more tokens in each sequence.

Attention now has a longer prefix to read. Recomputation also changes the work, and hardware utilization changes the time it takes. The estimate depends on which weights we count. Twenty presentations per parameter came from a particular training regime.

Start with two trillion extracted tokens. Quality filtering removes thirty percent, leaving one point four trillion. Deduplication removes twenty percent of that remainder, leaving one point one two trillion. If each surviving token is used once, how far short of the target are we?
We need two hundred eighty billion more presentations. We could add eligible sources or deliberately repeat some text. A bigger download helps only to the extent that its tokens reach training.

title: Will the return statement still run?

beats.say: Here is the page that supplied our program. Start with the whole response. Home and Subscribe belong to the menu. Links and Contact belong to the footer. Select the body between them. Two sentences and a Python function are worth keeping. What has to survive besides the words?

Copy the two sentences, including their final periods. Leave the navigation behind. Copy the function header, then its indented return statement. Try trimming every line. Python stops at line two because the function body must be indented. Copy the four leading spaces from the source. Now add two and three. The function returns five.
Other page types have different failure modes. Inspect tables and equations on their own sources.

Save the original page, its source ID and the versioned extraction policy. That lets us go back from record C to this very line. Inspect samples across source types before processing the crawl. If you start from somebody else's extracted text, their choices about spaces and punctuation have already reached you.

title: Choose which archived evidence reaches extraction

beats.say: Common Crawl offers three different artifacts for the same crawl. WARC preserves raw crawl records, including HTTP responses and page HTML. WAT stores computed metadata. WET stores automatically extracted plain text. Reading WET inherits the earlier extractor. Returning to WARC lets us make and version our own extraction choices.

The same source can supply broad web prose, a long argument, reference knowledge, code and tests, or a worked forum answer. Each has different license, formatting and curation needs. Keep snapshot, source identity and extracted spans attached.
Repository stars tell us how popular a project is. Follow the saved offsets back to the code. Read the function and look for a test that checks its result.

FineWeb and DataComp-LM tested extraction recipes in controlled training runs. Each did better with text extracted from WARC than with its WET baseline. Look at the two copies of our function. Find the plus sign in each. How far in does the word return start?
Line up the original and extracted return statements. Can you find the four spaces in both? Make the same comparison on tables and equations before choosing a faster extractor.

title: A quality rule chooses what remains

beats.say: These are all five records before deduplication. Even the two mirrors still count separately. The menu already falls below the starting cutoff of point two. A classifier learns from its examples and labels. A rule for repeated lines or empty pages can catch a different problem.

Raise the cutoff to point six nine. Nothing crosses it yet. Now move past the program's score and its one hundred twenty tokens leave. Move past E and another two hundred leave. At point eight five, only the two mirrors remain. Their mean score is higher.
That follows from discarding lower scores. To find out what the model learned, compare matched training runs.
Try a different policy. Reset the score cutoff to point five. Four records now qualify. Suppose we also require a prose source and at least two hundred tokens. Which additional record will we lose?

C drops out. The little program fails both parts of the prose rule. The two mirrors and the bird sentence survive. Now six hundred eighty tokens remain, all prose. We can test a code-specific rule against this one on the tasks the engineering assistant needs.

title: Apply a prose rule to the actual record

beats.say: Open the article’s executable prose filter. It is a teaching subset of Gopher’s English-web rules. It keeps fifty through one hundred thousand whitespace-split words and mean word length from three through ten characters. Each hash-symbol count divided by word count, and each ellipsis count divided by word count, must be at most zero point one.

Consider this runbook. Its seventy-one words include both “the” and “and.” The gate asks for at least two distinct English stopwords from its list. At least eighty percent of the words must also contain a letter. The runbook passes all the implemented checks.

The four-word note is too short. Eighty copies of sale clear the length check but have no listed stopwords. The CSS has twenty-five hash signs for one hundred twenty-five words. That's one in five, twice the allowed ratio. Only the runbook passes this filter.

The published suite also checks repeated lines, paragraphs and n-grams. Its top two-, three- and four-gram limits use character fractions of zero point two zero, zero point one eight and zero point one six, respectively; longer n-grams use separate duplicate-character rules. Our subset omits those checks.
Passing it establishes only those implemented gates. Code, mathematics and other languages need separately evaluated recipes.

title: Follow the labels behind a quality score

beats.say: A score means what its labels and reference data teach. Language identification routes text; uncertain multilingual text or code is not thereby gibberish. DataComp-LM’s fastText positives included OpenHermes and highly rated ELI5 answers. Its top-ten-percent document cutoff was one stage in a larger pipeline, not a ten-percent token-yield guarantee.

FineWeb-Edu used four hundred sixty thousand teacher annotations on a zero-to-five educational scale: four hundred ten thousand for training and fifty thousand for validation. Education labels are not factuality or coding certificates. CCNet’s Wikipedia-trained language models ranked reference-domain perplexity into tiers; low perplexity means proximity to that reference, not universal usefulness.

Try the scorer on these five records. The proof scores point nine eight. The API documentation scores point nine two. The strip widths show their token counts. Set the cutoff to point nine. The forum post, the news story and the scrape fall below it.

The proof and the documentation keep two hundred eighty of the thousand tokens, or twenty-eight percent. A higher cutoff can leave both the yield and the mean unchanged between records. Once you cross a record, you lose its tokens.
If any remain, their mean score can only stay the same or rise. To decide whether that trade helps, evaluate the tasks you need.

title: Separate corpus inventory from evidence of value

beats.say: C4 illustrates aggressive heuristic cleaning; the Pile documented a twenty-two-source mixture; Dolma made a large English corpus and its processing inspectable. FineWeb tested extraction, filtering and per-crawl deduplication, rather than choosing a recipe from raw size.
DataComp-LM’s multi-stage pipeline turned a two hundred forty trillion token pool into a much smaller selected inventory. Judge a source by its contribution under a matched evaluation.

Nemotron-CC combined retained organic web text with synthetic variants. Its full and high-quality subsets traded results differently across reported tasks. FineWeb2 later adapted language processing and quality thresholds across more than one thousand languages. Copying one English stopword rule into every language can remove the very coverage that the deployment needs.

The December twenty twenty-five Nemotron-CC version two point one card reports two point five trillion added English tokens across organic, translated and synthetically rephrased text, with dataset and teacher-model terms. Keep those categories separate.

A forecast of public human text depends on what sources and dates it counts. A training run can read the same text again. Keep three counts when planning a longer run: distinct human source tokens, generated variants, and the number of token presentations the model consumes.

title: Repeated pages spend repeated practice

beats.say: Look at the cat sentence in A and B. An identical page mirrored across several sites can receive many times the exposure of another document. Exact deduplication groups matching normalized content. In our inventory, the second copy vanishes and its source lineage remains connected to the retained representative.

Change one word in the cat sentence. Read each group of three consecutive words in both copies. Two of the six distinct triples occur in both. The near match survives an exact-byte screen. At scale, MinHash and locality-sensitive hashing nominate pairs for a separate similarity check.

A shared introduction does not make two complete documents interchangeable. Inspect what a deduplication policy removes, including repeated material within documents. Count both documents and tokens: dropping one long page can change the mixture more than dropping several short pages.

title: Construct the candidate signature from real shingles

beats.say: An exact hash still has to read every byte. After normalization we can look up the digest in expected constant time. Compare the grouped bytes to settle equality. Change one word in this policy and the digest changes. How much wording do the two versions still share?

Start with the first two words of each passage. Slide the window one word at a time. Put each distinct pair on the rail below its passage. The word need became require, so both pairs touching that word change. Security review still lines up at the end. Count the matching pairs, then count the different pairs across both rails.

Six pairs match out of ten distinct pairs. That gives a Jaccard similarity of zero point six. At scale we first need to find pairs worth checking. For each passage, hash every bigram with the same salt and keep the smallest hash. Repeat for thirty-two salts. Group four consecutive minima into each of eight bands.

Read each dot as a comparison between the two passages. Green means the minima agree. Compare the four rows of band one. They match all the way down. Band three also matches, so the pair becomes a candidate. Verify the original shingle sets. Six out of ten clears our inclusive point five threshold. Now draw the edge.

Keep A, the alphabetically first member of the component. Store B’s link to A. The audit-log passage C stays separate. With an ideal random permutation, the two minima match exactly when the smallest shingle in their union is shared. That happens with probability equal to Jaccard similarity. A finite salted hash approximates that ideal.

title: Which shingles survive a chain of matches?

beats.say: What makes two signatures worth comparing? All four rows in one band have to match. If each ideal independent row matches with probability s, one band matches with probability s to the fourth. Subtract the probability that all eight bands miss from one. Change the band count or the rows per band and the exponents change with them.
Follow the curve from a quarter similarity through one half to three quarters. At one half, about forty percent of pairs become candidates. Even a promising pair can miss every band.

Now take three different records. Each numbered tile stands for a shingle. The middle record contains all six. Verify the proposed pairs against a point six cutoff. A shares four of six with B. So does C. Both neighboring pairs pass at two thirds.
Compare the ends directly. A and C share just two of six, so their edge fails. Keep the alphabetically first record in each connected group. Which shingles will disappear?

Follow the green edges from A through B to C. All three belong to one group. Keep A and remove B and C. Five and six have disappeared. They were in B and C, and neither one was in A. Inspect what large components remove.
Crowded band buckets can also require a quadratic number of pair comparisons.

Check which recipe you intend to run. FineWeb used five-word shingles and one hundred twelve hashes, arranged in fourteen bands of eight. It linked band matches directly. Our example verifies Jaccard before adding an edge. FineWeb also compared per-crawl and global deduplication.
Which records survive depends on both the linking rule and the pool you compare.

title: How much did the mirror cost?

beats.say: Return to our five records. Each strip is as wide as its token count, measured with the same tokenizer. A and B are copies. C is our program. Use the point five cutoff with the extra prose rule switched off. Remove D, the two hundred menu tokens.
Eight hundred tokens remain. Before you drop B, what fraction of those remaining tokens does the mirror occupy?

B occupies two hundred forty of the eight hundred tokens. That's thirty percent at this step. Drop the mirror and close the gap. You can still trace B to A. Five hundred sixty tokens survive in three distinct records.
One of the four records disappeared at this step, but it took thirty percent of the tokens with it.

Suppose we budget seven hundred token presentations. Use each of these three records once and we're short one hundred forty. We can find more eligible text or schedule repeats. To see what repeats buy us, count what the sampler actually draws from each source.

title: How much practice fits in ten draws?

beats.say: For a separate sampler example, every program has one hundred tokens. Every prose page has nine hundred. Each tile holds one hundred tokens. The ten draw values are evenly spaced examples, from point zero five to point nine five. Draw a whole document each time.

Values below one half pick code. The first five programs make a low shelf. The next five pages stand nine tiles high. Five draws apiece gave code only five hundred of five thousand tokens. How many programs would balance one page?

It takes nine programs. Keep the same ten draws and raise the chance of picking code to ninety percent. Watch four tall columns turn into short ones. Nine programs now contribute nine hundred tokens, and so does the one remaining page.
In a random run it is the long-run share that balances. Multiply each source's draw probability by its mean retained length, then divide by the total expected tokens per draw.

Keep that ninety percent setting, but cut both sources into equal blocks of one hundred tokens. The last page now supplies just one tile per draw as well. To get half your tokens from code, how many of ten equal blocks should come from code?

Five code blocks. Set the probability back to one half. Each side supplies five hundred tokens. When all blocks have the same length and every token is kept, the source probability is also its expected token share. Measure consumed tokens after truncation and packing. Count supervised targets separately if the loss skips some positions.

title: A mixture changes what the model repeatedly practices

beats.say: The whole-document formula is source probability times mean retained length, divided by the sum of those products across sources. It assumes all sampled tokens survive.

With one hundred-token code and nine hundred-token prose, eighty percent code document draws give eighty expected code tokens versus one hundred eighty prose tokens per draw: only about thirty-one percent code tokens.

To target a desired token share, divide each desired share by that source’s mean document length, then normalize the resulting weights. Equal desired shares here require ninety percent code document draws. A sampler of equal-length token blocks has a different contract.
Source-specific truncation, packing and omitted loss targets can change the delivered or supervised mixture, so count those actual exposures.

Training stages can use different weights. The sampler can also choose different records within a source. Look at Llama three's reported token mix. General web gets half the tokens. Math and reasoning gets a quarter. Code gets seventeen percent, and multilingual text gets eight.

Now take a different plan. A hundred billion eligible code tokens supply seven hundred billion presentations. Divide the presentations by the inventory. That's seven token-weighted passes on average. Some programs may appear more often than others. Measure held-out behavior to decide whether more repetition helps.

title: Trace a candidate match into a versioned review

beats.say: Pin benchmark versions and splits before overlap screening. Known repository or domain exclusions catch obvious sources. Literal n-grams catch copied wording. Code-aware comparisons can propose renamed copies, while semantic retrieval can nominate paraphrases. Each stage has false positives and misses; no universal cosine threshold proves exposure.
A benchmark sentinel signals lineage, including documentation that quotes it, rather than proving that an answer entered training.

The executable screen uses an authored marker, exact four-word overlap and lexical code normalization. It flags the marker copy, the copied prompt and renamed code; the runbook has no implemented match and still needs residual auditing. Repository exclusions and embedding retrieval are proposed extensions outside this cell.
GPT-3’s initial thirteen-gram filter and later task-dependent overlap analysis also had documented implementation limits.

Look at the last return in each function. Our lexical screen removes comments and keeps a hash inside a quoted string. It also discards indentation and doesn't resolve scope. The normalized tokens are identical. In which function can a false flag reach the last return?

Call decide with False on both. On the left, execution leaves the if and returns two. On the right, both returns belong to the if. The function falls off the end and returns None. Send this match to policy review.
Save the matched span, the source and the benchmark revision. A shared passage and an exposed answer have different implications for the evaluation.

title: Apply identifier and secret policies to the retained source

beats.say: Useful technical text can contain private identifiers and leaked secrets. Define separate policies for structured identifiers, credentials and contextual personal information. A private key is a secret; a public name or IP address is not automatically private in every context. Track policy version and source spans before destructive tokenization or sharding makes inspection harder.

Regular expressions find some structured formats. Entity recognition can flag a name for contextual review. Source controls can exclude known leak sites. Replace the email with the literal text email in angle brackets. Check the next line: the private-key marker is still there. Hold this record for secret handling. The tokenizer treats our placeholder as ordinary text unless we register it as a special token.
Stable hashed identifiers can remain linkable and need their own policy.

Unsafe-content classifiers need the same error audit. A clinical explanation and an abusive message can share a flagged word while needing different decisions. Inspect retained and removed samples across intended groups and domains. A high quality score, successful deduplication or one scrubber pass establishes no privacy guarantee.
Check provenance, license and secret handling again when synthetic variants are added.

title: Count both the token stream and its vocabulary rows

beats.say: The tokenizer turns retained text into integer IDs. Vocabulary size changes both sequence compression and embedding or output cost. A vocabulary of V pieces with width d uses V times d entries in each dense vocabulary matrix.

If the input and output matrices have separate weights, both grow when we add rows. Add eight thousand rows at width two hundred fifty-six, with two bytes per entry. Across both matrices that costs just over eight million additional bytes. Tying the weights changes that count.

Byte-level BPE starts from byte values and learns frequent adjacent merges; representing all two hundred fifty-six byte values covers ordinary UTF-eight bytes. WordPiece uses greedy longest-match segmentation with a learned vocabulary.
Unigram fits piece probabilities and prunes candidates; SentencePiece is a library supporting BPE and Unigram, not a synonym for one algorithm. Pre-tokenization controls allowed merge boundaries.

The Llama three report measured English text. Llama two averaged three point one seven characters per token. Llama three averaged three point nine four. Now read the indented return line from our program. We ran its sixteen characters through a frozen tiktoken encoding. Each dot marks a space. Count the pieces as they separate. Include the piece made entirely of spaces. Five tokens cover the line. Sixteen divided by five gives three point two characters per token for this example. Repeat the measurement on each language and kind of code you serve. Before writing shards, freeze the tokenizer revision, normalization, merge ranks and special token IDs.

Which token contains the fourth space before return? Follow the last dot in the indent. It shares a token with the word return. This pre-tokenizer lets a leading space stay with the next word, and the merge rules join them here.

title: Replay the learned merge order on the actual word pieces

beats.say: This toy tokenizer splits on whitespace, then starts from Unicode characters plus an end-of-word marker. It has ninety-four initial symbols across the supplied corpus. Counting adjacent pairs, merging the most frequent, and repeating eight times leaves sixty-eight symbols.
We'll replay those rules on the four words rotate keys after review. They start with twenty-five symbols including their end markers. As each rule lands, count the pieces still on the strip.
Watch the word after. First join T and E. Follow the next two rules in rotate, where T joins A and R joins O. Now join A and F in after. Those first two pieces, AF and TE, can now join.

Add R and then the end marker. The entire word after occupies one piece. The last rule joins RO and TA in rotate. Now count the pieces in the four words. Sixteen remain. Each rule joins adjacent pieces from left to right without overlap.
We never count the new prompt's pairs to choose its next rule.

Tied counts follow first encounter order in this toy, so changing training-record order can change the rules. One emoji is one Unicode character here but four UTF-eight bytes. Whitespace splitting also discards the original spaces.

Our toy starts with characters and discards spaces. Decoding these pieces cannot recover the original spacing. Pin the tokenizer revision with the shards. If the revision changes, check compatibility before reusing them. Suppose only the documentation changed. For rotate, the pieces and their IDs still match. Now drop the last merge. Where we stored one piece for rota, the new tokenizer emits two. Retokenize the affected text. A change to ID assignments can also make stored IDs incompatible, even when the pieces look the same.

title: Conserve token slots while moving whole records

beats.say: Packing makes utilization visible. The supplied lengths are seven, six, five, five, three and two, each including whatever separators our declared fixture counts. Separate capacity-ten blocks allocate sixty slots for twenty-eight real tokens. Best-fit decreasing sorts lengths largest first and places each in the tightest block where it fits.

Deal the records from longest to shortest. Put seven in the first block. Six needs a second block. The two fives fit together in a third block. Where can the three go? Slide three beside seven. Put two beside six. You can still count the same twenty-eight real tokens.
They now occupy thirty slots, about ninety-three percent full. The separate records used only about forty-seven percent of their sixty slots.

Change the lengths. Now every record has six tokens. Each leaves four empty places, too few for another six. Eighteen of thirty slots are full, exactly sixty percent. Real packing also has to move token IDs and source offsets.

Count separators, bound the streaming buffer, and decide how to split an overlong document. Kernels can skip padding, so a slot count alone can't tell us how much compute we saved. Return to the first arrangement. A seven and a three share a block. Should they be able to read each other?

title: A packed stream needs a boundary policy

beats.say: Here are two short documents packed into one block of integer IDs. The cat sat ends the first document. Birds sing begins the second. Packing places short sequences together to save padding. This time we want each document to be an independent example. Look at Birds.
Which of the earlier words in this block can it read?

None of the earlier words. In this row, Birds can read only itself. The segment-aware causal mask admits keys in the same document up to the query position. Move to sing. It can read Birds and itself. Move to the end marker.
All three local positions are visible. The matrix marks the allowed edges. A position reset or an end marker alone cannot block earlier positions in another document.

Go back to sat, the final token of the first document. The next physical token in this block is Birds. A model trained on independent documents should skip that prediction across the boundary. We can mark its loss target as ignored.
An intentionally continuous text stream can choose a different convention. Let's see where that ignore value goes in two common training APIs.

title: Shift each target exactly once

beats.say: The article’s five input IDs are eleven, twelve, ninety-nine, twenty-one and ninety-nine. Document IDs are zero, zero, zero, one and one. Under the chosen independent-document objective, allow a key only when it is no later than the query and belongs to that same document.

Number the positions starting at zero. Query position three cannot read key position two. Translate that logical mask to the API’s boolean or additive convention. A logit multiplied by zero can still receive attention.

If the data pipeline supplies already-shifted next-token targets, they are twelve, ninety-nine, ignore, ninety-nine and ignore. The cross-document target and the final input without a next token are omitted. The common ignore value minus one hundred controls loss eligibility, not attention. There are three supervised predictions in this block.

If the model shifts labels internally, start from a copy of the inputs. Ignore the first label of the new document. Supply eleven, twelve, ninety-nine, ignore and ninety-nine. After one shift, the aligned targets are twelve, ninety-nine, ignore and ninety-nine. Count the supervised predictions. Follow each arrow and skip the ignored target. Three predictions receive loss in both layouts. A second shift would teach different targets.
Sequence boundaries can implement isolation without materializing the quadratic mask; position resets need a segment-aware attention path to enforce it.

title: A checkpoint needs the next document too

beats.say: Prepared shards should carry immutable identities, source policies, and tokenizer information. A manifest describes the files and their hashes. This turns a changing directory into a specific dataset artifact that another run can verify and load again.

Save each worker's progress and random state. The seed tells us where the order began. To resume this completed training step, restore the consumed cursor to two. That step consumed A and C. E is the next block to deliver.

Keep held-out evaluations separate from training preparation and check contamination against their contents. Related documents may need group-based splits. Privacy and license policies also belong in the pipeline, with inspectable decisions appropriate to the source and intended use.

title: Restore consumed work rather than the furthest read

beats.say: At scale, extraction and signatures can run independently across records; band-bucket grouping requires shuffling records to their common comparison owner. Packing then builds sequences under a deterministic policy. Size these stages from measured throughput, storage and shuffle traffic. A borrowed node count and a raw-token estimate do not establish input readiness.

This six-record sample saves a fingerprint and a shuffled order. An optimizer step has consumed zero and five. The reader has already fetched one and two into its buffer. If the job stops here, which record should the next step receive?

Resume at the consumed cursor. Deliver record one first. Record two follows, then three and four. Join that suffix to the saved prefix. Every record occurs once in the original order. A changed record fails the fingerprint check. For files, read every referenced shard and verify its bytes against its digest.

Leave the consumed cursor in place and look at the reader cursor farther along. If we restore the reader cursor, records one and two never reach training. If we restart from the seed alone, zero and five repeat. Save the intra-sequence offset, worker progress and random state at the completed optimizer step.
Restore model, optimizer and schedule together, and restore or deterministically regenerate prefetch and stochastic transforms. The small cell alone is not a complete distributed restart.

title: Control both the late mixture and its evidence

beats.say: Late-stage data annealing here pairs a learning-rate cooldown with a targeted source-mixture change. The Llama three report describes a linear decay to zero over its final forty million tokens, upsampling very high quality sources and averaging checkpoints. Its separate small annealing probes evaluate candidate data.
Compare candidate final mixtures from the same starting checkpoint and check both target gains and lost domain coverage.

Synthetic data can propose gap-filling exercises, explanations and formats. Phi-one combined filtered real code with synthetic textbooks and exercises, within its reported coding tasks. Here a generated exercise asks for the sum of two and three. A second example asks why the return is indented. Both come from the same real function. Counting those variants as new human inventory would count their source again.

Run the original function to check the proposed answer. It returns five. Preserve that source link, privacy decisions and the dataset and teacher terms. Use executable tests or source-supported checks to catch generated errors.

Recursive replacement can lose distribution tails under studied model-collapse assumptions. Accumulating original and generated data avoided collapse in Gerstgrasser and colleagues’ language-model experiments, with a separate bounded-error linear-model result. That does not certify every mixture or architecture.

Keep the original records and measure rare-domain coverage. Suppose the target score rises from point eight eight to point nine two. On a separate held-out domain, point eight four falls to point seven seven. Its declared floor is point eight. Hold this mixture and test a revised one from the common checkpoint.

title: What changed when the cutoff moved?

beats.say: Back to C, our little program. At point five, the unique inventory contains one hundred twenty code tokens. Let's follow four draws of a hundred tokens each. First take the start of C, then A. Take the same part of C again, then E. The model saw two hundred code token presentations, even though both code blocks came from the same hundred positions.
A source ID and offset let us trace that repeat.

Keep extraction and deduplication fixed. Raise only the cutoff. It crosses point seven and C drops out. Above point eight, E drops out too. Stop at point eight five. A remains, with two hundred forty tokens.
Weight each surviving score by its token count and the mean rises from about point eight two to point nine. Could this inventory supply a single code token, however often we draw from it?

There is no code left to draw. Compare two illustrative runs with the same starting checkpoint and training budget. Score them on the same ten held-out cases. Seven successes become five. Look at cases one and two. Both changed from a success to a miss.
We lost C and E together, so these results alone can't tell us which removal mattered. Restore C alone in the next trial, keep the budget fixed, and evaluate on fresh cases.

title: Would you release this training mix?

beats.say: Your turn. This batch has a program, some documentation, and a web page. All three pass at point seven. Each strip shows its score and its length in tokens. If you move the cutoff to point nine, how many of these six hundred tokens survive, and from which source?

Move the cutoff to point nine. It crosses code at point seven two, then web at point eight eight. The documentation stays. That's one hundred eighty of six hundred tokens, or thirty percent. Every retained token now comes from the record scored point nine four.

Here are results for two imagined runs from the same checkpoint, with the same training budget. Each task has twenty held-out cases. We agreed before training that code needs sixteen successes. At the stricter cutoff, the documentation score goes from sixteen to nineteen.
Code goes from seventeen to fifteen. The combined count improves by one. Would you release this mix?

Hold this mix. Code fell one success short of the release minimum. Three more documentation cases passed, but the code requirement still applies. Return to the rejected program. We can test whether restoring that source helps.

Leave docs and web at point nine. Lower just the code cutoff to point seven. That puts one hundred twenty code tokens back beside the documentation. Plan both runs from the same completed optimizer checkpoint. First verify the data state that produced it.

Two records were consumed and four were read. On the pinned stream the next two prefetched records still belong to training. Verify the shard bytes and tokenizer. When the new mixture starts, give it its own manifest and sampler state. Keep the training budget fixed and score both tasks on fresh held-out cases.

Will code reach sixteen out of twenty? The new evaluation will tell us. We can now trace a change in code exposure all the way back to the cutoff. In the next lab, the packed IDs and their shifted targets go into the decoder itself.
